slot.brief: For a body rolling without slipping, relate the velocity of a point on the rim (e.g., topmost or contact point) to the centre-of-mass velocity.

stem: A wheel rolls to the right without slipping. At an instant, the radius from its centre to a marked point on the rim is inclined at $60^\circ$ above the horizontal in the direction of motion. What is the direction of the point's velocity relative to the ground?

verdicts.working: For rolling right, the point’s rotational velocity has magnitude v and points 30° below horizontal. Adding the centre’s velocity v rightward gives tan θ = (v/2)/(v + √3v/2) = 2 − √3, hence θ = 15° below horizontal.

working:
Let the centre's velocity be $v\hat{i}$ and $\omega=v/R$ clockwise.
For $\vec{r}=R(\cos60^\circ\hat{i}+\sin60^\circ\hat{j})$, the rotational velocity is $\vec{\omega}\times\vec{r}=v(\sin60^\circ\hat{i}-\cos60^\circ\hat{j})$.
Thus $\vec{v}_P=v(1+\sin60^\circ)\hat{i}-v\cos60^\circ\hat{j}$.
$\tan\beta=\dfrac{\cos60^\circ}{1+\sin60^\circ}=2-\sqrt{3}=\tan15^\circ$.
So the velocity is directed $15^\circ$ below the horizontal.

Independent check: For rolling right, the point’s rotational velocity has magnitude v and points 30° below horizontal. Adding the centre’s velocity v rightward gives tan θ = (v/2)/(v + √3v/2) = 2 − √3, hence θ = 15° below horizontal.
solution:
For rolling without slipping, the centre’s speed is $v$ and the rim’s rotational speed is also $v$. At the marked point, the rotational velocity has components $v\sin60^\circ$ rightward and $v\cos60^\circ$ downward, so
$$\tan\beta=\frac{v\cos60^\circ}{v(1+\sin60^\circ)}=2-\sqrt3=\tan15^\circ.
$$Thus the point moves $15^\circ$ below the horizontal.
